# Claude Opus 5.5 is now available in GitHub Copilot

 

Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic’s newest Opus model, is now available in GitHub Copilot. You can use it for agentic coding, long-running agentic tasks, and knowledge work. In early testing, Opus 5.5 resolved tasks comparably to Claude Opus 5 while using significantly fewer steps and tokens. It also quickly recovered from errors in multistep tasks.

Claude Opus 5.5 watermarks its text outputs. The watermark doesn’t change the meaning, quality, or readability of outputs, nor does it add any tokens or cost. To learn more visit Anthropics’s How Claude’s text watermark works.

This model is billed at provider list pricing under usage-based billing. See Models and pricing for GitHub Copilot for details.

### Availability in GitHub Copilot

Claude Opus 5.5 is available to Copilot Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise users. You can select the model in the model picker in:

- Visual Studio Code
- Visual Studio
- Copilot CLI
- GitHub Copilot coding agent
- GitHub Copilot app
- github.com
- GitHub Mobile on iOS and Android
- JetBrains IDEs
- Xcode
- Eclipse

Rollout will be gradual. Check back soon if you don’t see it yet.

### Enabling access

Copilot Enterprise and Copilot Business plan administrators can manage access to Claude Opus 5.5 through the model policy in Copilot settings. Under default model enablement, new models are automatically enabled unless an administrator has turned off the global default or explicitly disables this model.

### Learn more

To explore all models available in GitHub Copilot, see our documentation on models and get started with Copilot.

## GitHub Copilot's October 2 model cutover swaps Claude Opus 4.7's replacement to Opus 5.5

October 3, 2026 · by Pondero Newsdesk

GitHub's October 2 changelog confirmed the removal of Gemini 3.5/3.6 Flash, Kimi K2.7 Code, and Claude Opus 4.7 from Copilot, pointing admins to Opus 5.5 instead of the Opus 5 named a month earlier.

# GitHub Copilot's October 2 model cutover swaps Claude Opus 4.7's replacement to Opus 5.5

GitHub finished a deprecation it announced a month ago, and the model it is steering admins toward has changed since that first notice. On September 3, GitHub told Copilot admins that Claude Opus 4.7 would retire October 2 in favor of Claude Opus 5. The October 2 changelog that actually carried out the cutover names a different target: Claude Opus 5.5.

## What happened

As of October 2, 2026, GitHub deprecated four models across every Copilot surface, including Chat, inline edits, ask and agent modes, and code completions, per the GitHub changelog. Both Gemini 3.5 Flash and Gemini 3.6 Flash give way to Gemini 3.8 Flash, and Kimi K2.7 Code hands off to Kimi K3. The fourth retirement carries the real change: Claude Opus 4.7's replacement is now Claude Opus 5.5, not the Claude Opus 5 that GitHub's September 3 notice had named a month earlier. GitHub said no admin action is required to remove the old models; they stay selectable in the Chat model picker without manual cleanup, just unsupported. Enterprise and Business admins who want the replacements available still have to turn them on through their organization's Copilot model policy before the new model shows up in the selector.

## Policies tuned for Opus 5 in September need a second look

Any admin who read the September notice literally and enabled Opus 5 specifically in their model policy has not actually provisioned the model GitHub now recommends. Anthropic shipped Opus 5.5, and GitHub added it to Copilot across every IDE surface on September 22, weeks after the original deprecation notice went out. The swap matters most for teams that locked workflows or Copilot Extensions to a named model string. Those integrations do not fail silently; they stop resolving once the underlying model is gone, so the fix is to re-check the model policy against today's changelog rather than the one from a month ago.

## What to watch next

Kimi K3 taking over as Copilot's suggested replacement for code-focused tasks lands in an awkward week for its maker. OpenAI disclosed on October 2 that it disrupted a reasoning-extraction campaign it ties to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, according to the report. GitHub has not said whether that dispute affects Kimi K3's standing inside Copilot, and nothing in the October 2 changelog suggests it will. Worth checking is whether GitHub's model-policy UI already lists Opus 5.5 and Kimi K3 as available, or whether rollout lags the changelog entry for some tiers.

## Sources

- Selected models in GitHub Copilot deprecated: GitHub changelog, October 2, 2026
- Upcoming deprecation of selected GitHub Copilot models: GitHub changelog, September 3, 2026
- OpenAI Disrupts Reasoning Extraction Campaign Linked to Moonshot AI Associates: The Hacker News, October 2, 2026

# GitHub Copilot model deprecations: what admins must approve before 19 October

GitHub Copilot retires GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4 and four more models on 19 October 2026. Which replacements need admin approval, and how to enable them.

HighCircl Editorial Team

October 5, 2026

GitHub Copilot model deprecations: what admins must approve before 19 October

GitHub Copilot retires GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4 and four more models on 19 October 2026. Which replacements need admin approval, and how to enable them.

HighCircl Editorial Team

GitHub Copilot's next model deprecation lands on 19 October 2026, when six models go away, and the replacements only switch on by themselves for some admins. If you turned off default model enablement, or explicitly disabled a model, nothing replaces it until you approve the successor. A first wave of four models already went on 2 October, so the same check applies today. For the wider picture of what model changes mean for engineering teams, see AI model releases and pricing: what changes for engineering teams.

## Which Copilot models are being removed, and what replaces them

GitHub's September 18 changelog on mid-October deprecations names six models for removal on 19 October 2026. The October 2 changelog on deprecated models covers four more that are already gone.

| Deprecated model | Replacement | Removed on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gemini 3.5 Flash | Gemini 3.8 Flash | 2 October 2026 (done) |
| Gemini 3.6 Flash | Gemini 3.8 Flash | 2 October 2026 (done) |
| Kimi K2.7 Code | Kimi K3 | 2 October 2026 (done) |
| Claude Opus 4.7 | Claude Opus 5.5 | 2 October 2026 (done) |
| Gemini 3.7 Flash | Gemini 3.8 Flash | 19 October 2026 |
| GPT-5.5 | GPT-5.6 Sol | 19 October 2026 |
| GPT-5.4 | GPT-5.6 Sol | 19 October 2026 |
| GPT-5.4 mini | GPT-5.6 Luna | 19 October 2026 |
| GPT-5 mini | GPT-5.6 Luna | 19 October 2026 |
| Grok 4.5 | Grok 4.6 | 19 October 2026 |

Four distinct replacements cover the second wave: GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Luna, Gemini 3.8 Flash and Grok 4.6. Those are the ones to put in front of whoever owns your model policy. Gemini 3.8 Flash replaces three removed models across both waves, which makes it the one most teams will touch first. Its pricing is covered in our Gemini 3.8 Flash pricing write-up.

## Who has to act: default model enablement on or off

The September 18 changelog says that for Copilot Enterprise and Business, "Under default model enablement, the suggested alternatives are automatically enabled" unless an administrator has turned off the global default or explicitly disabled the model. That condition sorts admins into three cases.

If default model enablement is on and nothing is disabled, replacements are enabled automatically. They appear in the model selector in Chat, inline edits, ask and agent modes, and code completions. You don't need to do anything, though it's worth knowing which new providers just reached your developers.

If the global default is turned off, the replacement stays off until you enable it. Developers still on a removed model lose it on 19 October, and the successor isn't there to pick up the slack.

If an administrator has explicitly disabled the model, the changelog says the alternatives aren't automatically enabled. The sentence doesn't say whether "the model" means the retiring model or its replacement, so check the policy status of both.

The October 2 changelog states the admin duty plainly: "Copilot Enterprise administrators may need to enable access to alternative models through their model policies in Copilot settings." It also says "No action is required to remove the deprecated models." What a developer sees when selecting a removed model isn't described in either changelog. The likely result in the second and third cases is a model picker with neither the old model nor its replacement, but that's inference, not something GitHub states.

# GitHub Copilot model deprecations: what business teams should review

GitHub’s Copilot model changes show why developer AI model choices should be treated as operational dependencies, not permanent features.

By OUROPT LTD Published 2 October 2026 3 min read

GitHub Copilot model deprecations mean teams using affected models should review the continuity of the developer workflows and integrations that depend on them. A suggested replacement may be a sensible starting point, but it is not evidence that results, access or commercial impact will be identical for every use case.

## What changed

In a GitHub changelog entry dated 2 October 2026, GitHub said it had deprecated Gemini 3.5 Flash, Gemini 3.6 Flash, Kimi K2.7 Code and Claude Opus 4.7 across GitHub Copilot experiences. The notice includes Copilot Chat, inline edits, ask and agent modes, and code completions.

GitHub suggested Gemini 3.8 Flash for the two deprecated Gemini models, Kimi K3 for Kimi K2.7 Code, and Claude Opus 5.5 for Claude Opus 4.7. It also asked users to move workflows and integrations to supported models. The announcement does not establish that these alternatives will perform equivalently in every organisation or task.

## Why this is a business issue, not only a developer-tool change

Where a team has built habits, internal processes or product work around a chosen model, a model withdrawal can affect predictability. The material question is not simply whether another model is listed; it is whether the organisation can still achieve the required quality, review standard and operational outcome without disrupting planned work.

- Which important development, support or product workflows rely on a named Copilot model or model-specific behaviour?
- Whether the proposed alternative is permitted and available under the organisation’s Copilot policies.
- Whether output quality or consistency could change for higher-risk tasks, including work that requires human review.
- Whether model choice has become an unrecorded dependency in supplier, product or delivery planning.
- Whether teams need clearer ownership for monitoring changes to AI-enabled tools.

## A suggested alternative is not a like-for-like assurance

Vendor recommendations are useful compatibility signals, but they should not be treated as a guarantee of comparable outputs, cost exposure, availability or suitability. The supplied announcement gives no evidence on those questions. Business teams should therefore avoid making assumptions about performance or commercial impact from the replacement name alone.

## Governance questions worth raising

- Do we know which AI tool and model choices are material to delivery continuity?
- Who decides whether a model change is acceptable for a workflow with customer, security or quality implications?
- Are human review expectations still appropriate if the underlying model changes?
- Can the organisation distinguish an optional productivity preference from a dependency that could affect commitments?
- Do internal policies allow access to the alternative model named by the provider?

## What GitHub says administrators may need to consider

GitHub states that Copilot Enterprise administrators may need to enable access to alternative models through model policies. It also says no action is required to remove the deprecated models. These are platform-specific statements, not a substitute for an organisation’s own assessment of the workflows affected by the change.

The practical lesson is broader than this one announcement: AI model selection should be documented as an operational choice where it influences delivery, quality controls or supplier dependency.

GitHub Copilot retires 4 models, including Claude Opus 4.7

# GitHub Copilot deprecates four models: what replaces each one and where

GitHub removed Gemini 3.5 and 3.6 Flash, Kimi K2.7 Code and Claude Opus 4.7 from Copilot on October 2, 2026. Replacements, plan limits and admin steps.

Edited by Hamza Ahmad Aslam Published Oct 5, 2026 Updated Oct 5, 2026 4 min read 3 sources

GitHub deprecated four models across GitHub Copilot on October 2, 2026: Gemini 3.5 Flash, Gemini 3.6 Flash, Kimi K2.7 Code and Claude Opus 4.7. The change took effect the day it was announced and covers Copilot Chat, inline edits, ask and agent modes, and code completions. GitHub names a replacement for each model and says users do not need to do anything to remove the old ones.

## Which Copilot models are gone and what replaces them

The GitHub changelog entry (opens in a new tab) gives one date, 2026-10-02, for all four models, with these suggested alternatives:

| Deprecated model | Suggested alternative |
| --- | --- |
| Gemini 3.5 Flash | Gemini 3.8 Flash |
| Gemini 3.6 Flash | Gemini 3.8 Flash |
| Kimi K2.7 Code | Kimi K3 |
| Claude Opus 4.7 | Claude Opus 5.5 |

GitHub's supported models reference (opens in a new tab) now lists all four in its model retirement history with a retirement date of 2026-10-02. There, the suggested alternatives are worded more generally: "Latest Claude Opus model", "Latest Gemini Flash model" and "Latest Kimi model". The changelog uses the word deprecated, but the docs file them as retired, and neither page mentions a grace period.

## What Copilot users need to do

Individual users mostly need to check saved choices. If a workflow, prompt file, custom agent or integration names one of the four models, it should point to a supported model instead. GitHub's note says the deprecated models disappear without any action on your part.

Copilot Enterprise administrators have a specific task. The replacement models may be switched off by model policy, so admins may need to enable them in Copilot settings. GitHub suggests checking your own Copilot settings to confirm the policy is on for each model. Once a policy is enabled, the model shows up in the Copilot Chat model picker in VS Code and on github.com. Enterprise customers with questions are pointed to their account manager.

## Where the replacement models are available

The supported models reference shows some differences between the old and new options that matter in practice.

Claude Opus 5.5 is marked GA. The plan table lists it for Copilot Pro+, Max, Business and Enterprise, but not for Copilot Pro. A Copilot Pro user who relied on Opus 4.7 therefore has no direct Opus replacement on that plan, based on the current table. Opus 5.5 is listed in every client in the per-client table, from GitHub.com to Xcode and JetBrains IDEs.

Gemini 3.8 Flash is also GA and is listed on all five plans. The per-client table marks it as available in Copilot CLI, VS Code, Visual Studio, Eclipse, Xcode and JetBrains IDEs, but not on GitHub.com. That sits awkwardly with the changelog's general line about models appearing on github.com once enabled.

Kimi K3 is GA, on all five plans and in every listed client. Kimi K3 and Claude Opus 5.5 both support the 1 million token context window and configurable reasoning levels. Gemini 3.8 Flash is not in that extended-capabilities table. GitHub notes that the 1 million token window works only in VS Code and Copilot CLI.

For IDE versions, the docs list Visual Studio 17.14.22 or 18.1.0 for Gemini 3.8 Flash, Visual Studio 17.14.6 for Claude Opus 5.5, and VS Code v1.131 for Kimi K3. Other entries are marked TBD.

## What the replacements cost

Copilot bills usage above plan allowances in AI credits, where 1 AI credit is $0.01 USD. GitHub's models and pricing page (opens in a new tab) lists these rates per 1 million tokens:

- Claude Opus 5.5: $4.00 input, $0.20 cached input, $5.00 cache write, $20.00 output.
- Kimi K3: $3.00 input, $0.30 cached input,

# GitHub Copilot Deprecates Four Models Including Claude Opus 4.7

GitHub Copilot dropped Gemini 3.5/3.6 Flash, Kimi K2.7 Code, and Claude Opus 4.7 as of October 2, 2026. Here's what to switch to and how admins enable replacements.

By James Calloway

## Changelog

- * Four models deprecated across all Copilot experiences as of October 2, 2026: Gemini 3.5 Flash, Gemini 3.6 Flash, Kimi K2.7 Code, and Claude Opus 4.7.
- * Suggested replacements are Gemini 3.8 Flash, Kimi K3, and Claude Opus 5.5.
- * Copilot Enterprise admins may need to enable alternative models via model policies in Copilot settings; no action is needed to remove deprecated models.

If your Copilot workflow leans on Claude Opus 4.7, Kimi K2.7 Code, or either of the recent Gemini Flash models, it's time to adjust. As of October 2, 2026, GitHub has deprecated four models across every Copilot surface — Chat, inline edits, ask mode, agent mode, and code completions. No partial rollout, no grace period mentioned in the announcement. The deprecation hits all experiences at once.

Here's the full list of what's gone and where GitHub points you next:

| Deprecated model | Deprecation date | Suggested alternative |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gemini 3.5 Flash | 2026-10-02 | Gemini 3.8 Flash |
| Gemini 3.6 Flash | 2026-10-02 | Gemini 3.8 Flash |
| Kimi K2.7 Code | 2026-10-02 | Kimi K3 |
| Claude Opus 4.7 | 2026-10-02 | Claude Opus 5.5 |

The Gemini consolidation is the least surprising entry on the list. Two Flash generations collapsing into Gemini 3.8 Flash is standard fast-model churn — if you had automations pinned to 3.5 or 3.6, the migration path is a one-line change and, frankly, you were probably due for it anyway. The Kimi K2.7 Code to K3 jump follows the same pattern: a version bump, a newer model, move along.

Claude Opus 4.7 is the one that will sting some teams. Opus remains the go-to pick for developers who want maximum reasoning quality on hard refactors and gnarly agent tasks, and if you've tuned prompts or agent behavior around 4.7's output characteristics, you'll want to re-run your evals against Opus 5.5 before you assume parity. GitHub's suggested alternative is the direct successor, so the switch should be mechanical — but "should be" has burned plenty of teams before.

## What you actually need to do

For most users: update your workflows and integrations to call the supported models. That's it. GitHub states plainly that no action is required to remove the deprecated models — they simply stop being available.

Copilot Enterprise administrators have one extra step. Alternative models may need to be explicitly enabled through model policies in Copilot settings. The verification procedure GitHub describes:

1. Open your individual Copilot settings.
2. Confirm the policy is enabled for the specific model you want.
3. Check the Copilot Chat model selector in VS Code or on github.com — once the policy is live, the model appears there.

If a replacement model doesn't show up in the picker, the policy is the first thing to check. Don't file a bug report before you've ruled out your own admin config.

GitHub Enterprise customers with questions or concerns are encouraged to contact their account manager.

## Context worth having

Model churn at this pace is now the norm for Copilot. GitHub has been rotating third-party models in and out of the lineup on a steady cadence, and deprecations bundled like this — multiple vendors, single date, clear successor for each — look designed to keep the supported list tight rather than to strand anyone. The pattern also signals where the lineup is heading: newer Flash-tier models for speed-sensitive work like completions, and current-generation flagship models for chat, agent mode, and complex edits.
